**My thinking:**

I am 75 years old. My back aches and my knees are not what they were. My son moved to the city years ago. I still work my land because what else would I do — this land is my life. I have about 4 mu.

I have grown wheat and maize my whole life. My father grew wheat and maize. Everyone in the village grows wheat and maize. This is what the land here is for. The soil is flat and the wells are still good enough, though deeper than before. I would not dare try something new at my age. If something fails, I cannot recover from it.

For wheat — it is already in the ground from last October, the way it always is. Now in spring I will water it at jointing stage, maybe again at heading. I will put urea on it like always. I will spray once or twice if I see the rust spots. I hire the neighbor's tractor for the rotary till and the harvester at harvest time. I cannot operate machines anymore.

After wheat comes off in June, I will plant maize right away in the same fields. I buy the hybrid seeds from the village supply shop — everyone does, they yield better. I press them into the stubble with the hand planter. The rains usually help in summer but I will pump once if it's dry at tasseling. I will put compound fertilizer down at planting.

I keep a small vegetable plot by the house — garlic and some cabbage — but that is just for eating, not for the plan.

Fertilizer rates are set by habit and local custom — urea topdressed on wheat at jointing, compound fertilizer pressed into maize stubble at seeding. He irrigates wheat three times in spring at jointing, heading, and grain-filling, and pumps once for maize only if summer rainfall is short. He sprays wheat twice against rust and aphids based on visual observation. All mechanized field operations — rotary tillage, seeding, harvesting — are contracted out to neighbors or local service teams because he can no longer operate machinery himself. No new crops are tried; stability and familiarity matter far more than optimization at this stage of life."
